Where RL Breaks: Localizing and Repairing
Failures via Targeted Continued Pretraining

Xinyi Wang Danqi Chen wangxinyilinda@gmail.com danqic@princeton.edu
Princeton Language and Intelligence
Abstract

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is widely used to improve reasoning in language models, yet growing evidence suggests that it mostly sharpens what the base model can already do. This raises a practical question: when RL fails, what is the base model missing? We look inside the RL policy’s own rollouts and find that failures are localized: whether a rollout fails is strongly predicted by a small set of characteristic nn-grams, ranging from reflection phrases such as let’s recheck to specific operations such as the inverse of A. These failures persist throughout RL training, although they are not beyond the model’s reach: other sampled answers to the same question are often correct. Building on this observation, we use the failure nn-grams to retrieve text from the pretraining corpus and continue pretraining the base model on it before RL. The resulting corpus has only 35M tokens, 3–4 orders of magnitude smaller than typical mid-training. We evaluate this approach on OLMo2 and Qwen3 models trained with RL on (1) GSM8K; (2) a mixture of math, commonsense, and knowledge questions; and (3) general math and science reasoning. Despite its size, the corpus yields consistent gains: our approach outperforms continued pretraining on the same amount of text sampled from the pretraining corpus across 10 out of 11 settings, including by 2.02.0 points on GSM8K when inserted before mid-training. The retrieved text also transfers across model families: text retrieved for OLMo2-1B’s failures improves Qwen3-4B on the mixture by 1.91.9 points over the same baseline. Together, our results suggest that where RL fails is a cheap and effective signal for selecting pretraining data. 11 1 Our code is released at https://github.com/WANGXinyiLinda/where-rl-breaks

1 Introduction

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become the dominant recipe for improving reasoning in language models. Yet growing evidence suggests that it largely sharpens what the base model can already do: it makes successful solutions more likely and failing ones less likely, but rarely produces solutions the base model could not already sample (Yue et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025). Prolonged or curriculum RL can go further (Liu et al., 2025; Cai et al., 2026), but the base model still sets the limit: RL builds new strategies only from skills the base model already has (Cheng et al., 2025), and its gains depend on what pretraining provides (Zhang et al., 2026; Shen et al., 2026; Foster et al., 2025). This raises a practical question: when RL fails, what exactly is the base model missing, and can we supply it before RL?

Prior work has approached this question from two separate directions. One line studies where in a reasoning trace RL has its effect or where things go wrong: RL updates concentrate on a small fraction of high-entropy tokens (Wang et al., 2025b), and a single token can mark where a reasoning trace turns toward failure (Ko et al., 2026). These findings have been used to change the training objective (Ko et al., 2026), but not to choose training data. The other line improves the base model with data before RL. Most prominently, mid-training on hundreds of billions of reasoning-heavy tokens, now a standard stage in open training recipes (Team Olmo et al., 2025), makes base models far more responsive to RL (Wang et al., 2025d); continued pretraining on text rich in reasoning behaviors such as verification and backtracking has a similar effect (Gandhi et al., 2025). These corpora, however, are chosen by task similarity or by hand, not by what a particular model gets wrong. We connect the two directions: like mid-training, we change the data before RL, but we use a model’s RL failures to select a small, targeted corpus.

We approach this question by asking where within a rollout RL fails. Our central observation is that failures are not diffuse: whether a rollout leads to an incorrect outcome is strongly predicted by whether it contains one of a small number of characteristic nn-grams (e.g., the small set of RL-critical tokens of Wang et al., 2025b and the single-token failure triggers of Ko et al., 2026). Which nn-grams are diagnostic depends on the model and the task: reflection and self-correction phrases (let’s recheck, there’s a mistake in the problem) for weak models on elementary math, where the model reflects and then spirals rather than recovers; and specific operations (convert the given matrix to reduced row echelon form, the inverse of A) for stronger models on broad reasoning suites. In both cases, the nn-gram does not cause the failure; it is a visible sign that the rollout has reached a point from which it rarely recovers. RL has little to learn from at such points: it improves the model only from rollouts the model itself samples, and rollouts that reach these points rarely succeed.

These failures are also not beyond the model’s reach: for nearly half of the questions with a failing rollout, another sampled answer to the same question is correct. This suggests that what the base model lacks is specific, and that a small amount of the right data could supply it. Our approach follows directly (Figure 1): we use the failure nn-grams as exact-match queries over the pretraining and mid-training corpora (Olmo-mix and Dolmino-mix; Walsh et al., 2025), continue pretraining the base model on the retrieved text, and re-run the same RL recipe. We evaluate on OLMo2 (Walsh et al., 2025) and Qwen3 (Yang et al., 2025) models trained with RL on (1) GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021); (2) a mixture of math, commonsense, and knowledge questions (GSM8K, Social IQA, MMLU, and TriviaQA; Sap et al., 2019; Hendrycks et al., 2021; Joshi et al., 2017); and (3) general math and science reasoning (Ma et al., 2025), inserting continued pretraining either on the released base model or, for OLMo2, before mid-training. Our contributions are:

  • •

    Where RL fails. RL failures concentrate on a small set of failure nn-grams whose content varies with the model and task, from reflection phrases to specific operations. These failures persist throughout RL, even when the model can answer the same question correctly (Sections 4.2 and 4.4).

  • •

    A small, targeted fix. Retrieving pretraining text with the failure nn-grams yields a 3535M-token corpus, 3–4 orders of magnitude smaller than mid-training, selected by the model’s own failures (Section 3.4).

  • •

    Consistent gains that transfer. Our approach outperforms continued pretraining on the same amount of text sampled from the same corpus in 10 of 11 settings, including by 2.02.0 points on GSM8K when inserted before mid-training (3 RL seeds). A corpus mined from OLMo2-1B’s failures improves Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-4B by up to 2.42.4 points.

2 Related Work

Does RL expand or amplify base-model reasoning?

RLVR drives progress in reasoning models (Guo et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2024), but whether it expands or merely sharpens the base model is contested. Evidence for sharpening includes pass@1 gains without pass@kk gains (Yue et al., 2025), convergence toward pretraining-favored distributions (Zhao et al., 2025), updates concentrated at a few high-entropy tokens (Wang et al., 2025b), and gains from uninformative rewards when the base model already has a strategy (Shao et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026); when rare correct trajectories vanish, pass@kk can even shrink (Zhou, 2026; Yuan et al., 2026). Counter-evidence shows the ceiling is partly a measurement artifact (Wen et al., 2026) and that prolonged or curriculum RL can move it (Liu et al., 2025; Cai et al., 2026). Work on both sides finds that RL composes only skills the base model already has (Cheng et al., 2025) and that gains are predicted by pretraining headroom (Shen et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026; Foster et al., 2025). Rather than changing RL, we ask which capability the base model lacks and supply it on the pretraining side.

Mid-training and continued pretraining for RL.

A growing body of work inserts a mid-training phase between pretraining and RL: hundreds of billions of math-heavy and chain-of-thought tokens can make Llama as RL-friendly as Qwen (Wang et al., 2025d), open recipes ship such a stage (Walsh et al., 2025; Team Olmo et al., 2025), and controlled studies find mid-training worth more than RL alone (Zhang et al., 2026). Variants place reasoning data in pretraining itself (Wang et al., 2025a; Akter et al., 2026), run RL during mid-training (Li et al., 2026; Tian et al., 2026), use an RL-tuned model to shape mid-training data (Huang et al., 2026; RRV et al., 2026), or prime a base model by continued pretraining on verification and backtracking behaviors (Gandhi et al., 2025; Shah et al., 2025). We share the premise that the repair belongs before RL but differ in signal and scale: the model’s own failure nn-grams select a corpus 3–4 orders of magnitude smaller. Continual-pretraining studies show that re-warming on a converged model first raises loss on the original distribution and that replay limits forgetting (Gupta et al., 2023; Ibrahim et al., 2024; Abbes et al., 2025); Section 4.3 shows the same effect.

Pretraining data selection and failure localization.

Selecting data for a target capability ranges from nn-gram importance resampling (Xie et al., 2023) to gradient- and influence-based methods (Xia et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2024; Humane et al., 2025); complementary work traces behavior to pretraining documents (Wang et al., 2025c; Ruis et al., 2025). Our retrieval is a lightweight instance (exact-match lookup via infini-gram; Liu et al., 2024), but the signal is new: markers of where a trained model breaks down, not similarity to a target task. On the failure side (see Song et al., 2026, for a survey), intrinsic self-correction is unreliable without external signal (Huang et al., 2024; Kamoi et al., 2024), “recheck” steps are overwhelmingly confirmatory (Long et al., 2026), and excess reflection surfaces as overthinking (Sui et al., 2025), consistent with the reflection phrases among our failure nn-grams. Closest to our diagnosis, Ko et al. (2026) identify single cliff tokens at which success probability drops and repair them with preference optimization; our failure nn-grams are the state-level, model-specific analogue mined from RL rollouts, and we use them to retrieve pretraining data rather than shape the RL objective.

3 Method

Our method has three parts (Figure 1). We first run RL and read off its rollouts a small set of failure nn-grams, phrases whose presence in a rollout predicts failure (Section 3.2). We then argue that RL does little to repair the states these phrases mark, because an on-policy objective learns how to continue from them only through the few successful continuations it samples there (Section 3.3). Finally, we use the failure nn-grams as retrieval queries over the pretraining corpus, continue pretraining on the retrieved text, and re-run the same RL recipe; a matched control runs the same pipeline with content-neutral queries (Section 3.4).

3.1 Preliminaries

We consider a reasoning task with prompts x∼𝒟x\sim\mathcal{D} and a verifier that assigns each rollout yy, a reasoning trace followed by an answer, a binary reward r⁡(x,y)∈{0,1}r(x,y)\in\{0,1\}. We post-train the base model π0\pi_{0} with GRPO (Shao et al., 2024). For each prompt, GG rollouts y1,…,yGy_{1},\dots,y_{G} are sampled from the current policy πθold\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}, and each receives the group-relative advantage A^i=(r⁡(x,yi)−meanj​r​(x,yj))/stdj​r​(x,yj)\hat{A}_{i}=\big(r(x,y_{i})-\mathrm{mean}_{j}\,r(x,y_{j})\big)/\mathrm{std}_{j}\,r(x,y_{j}), which is shared by all of its tokens and is zero when all GG rewards are equal. The policy is updated to maximize

𝒥(θ)=𝔼x,{yi}[1G∑i=1G1|yi|∑t=1|yi|min(ρi,tA^i,clip(ρi,t,1−ϵ,1+ϵ)A^i)]−β𝔻KL[πθ∥π0]\mathcal{J}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x,\{y_{i}\}}\Big[\tfrac{1}{G}\textstyle\sum_{i=1}^{G}\tfrac{1}{|y_{i}|}\sum_{t=1}^{|y_{i}|}\min\big(\rho_{i,t}\hat{A}_{i},\;\mathrm{clip}(\rho_{i,t},1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)\hat{A}_{i}\big)\Big]-\beta\,\mathbb{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}\big[\pi_{\theta}\,\|\,\pi_{0}\big] (1)

where ρi,t=πθ​(yi,t∣x,yi,<t)/πθold​(yi,t∣x,yi,<t)\rho_{i,t}=\pi_{\theta}(y_{i,t}\mid x,y_{i,<t})/\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(y_{i,t}\mid x,y_{i,<t}) is the token-level importance ratio, ϵ\epsilon the clipping range, and β\beta the weight of a KL penalty toward π0\pi_{0} (values, including the asymmetric clipping used for General Reasoner, are in Appendix B). We write πRL\pi_{\mathrm{RL}} for the resulting policy. Because advantages are estimated only from rollouts the policy itself samples, RL learns how to act in a given state only from the continuations it samples there; Section 3.3 returns to this point.

3.2 Localizing failures with nn-grams

We treat nn-grams as cheap, observable markers of rollout states and ask which ones are diagnostic of failure. An nn-gram gg is a span of nn consecutive tokens, such as let’s recheck, and Eg​(y)=𝟙​[g​ appears in ​y]E_{g}(y)=\mathbbm{1}[\,g\text{ appears in }y\,] indicates that rollout yy contains it. Over the rollouts of a fixed policy, we measure the conditional accuracy of the rollouts that contain gg,

a⁡(g)=Pr⁡[r⁡(x,y)=1|Eg​(y)=1].a(g)\;=\;\Pr\big[\,r(x,y)=1\;\big|\;E_{g}(y)=1\,\big]. (2)

We use πRL\pi_{\mathrm{RL}} rather than π0\pi_{0}, since its rollouts show the failures that remain after RL. This quantity is associational: whether a rollout emits let’s recheck is itself an outcome of the model’s state, so a⁡(g)a(g) measures how strongly gg marks a low-accuracy state, not the effect of inserting gg. This suffices to localize failures.

Concretely, we mine nn-grams from the reasoning spans of πRL\pi_{\mathrm{RL}}’s training rollouts, keep those that occur at least 20 times and in at least 0.1%0.1\% of the rollouts, remove candidates dominated by digits or formatting, merge near-duplicates into their longest common span, and rank the rest by a⁡(g)a(g). The lowest-accuracy phrases form the failure set 𝒢\mathcal{G}, which also serves as the set of retrieval queries.22 2 Across settings, nn ranges from 3 to 6 and 𝒢\mathcal{G} contains 4 to 20 queries; Appendix C lists every query verbatim. For the main OLMo2-1B GSM8K results, we use four representative queries chosen from the top 40 nn-grams, which contain many near-duplicates.

3.3 Diagnosis: localized low-value states

We view a rollout as a trajectory through latent reasoning states: after emitting tt tokens, the model is in a state sts_{t} that summarizes the prefix so far. The value of a state under policy π\pi,

Vπ​(s)=Pr⁡[eventual success∣s],V^{\pi}(s)=\Pr[\,\text{eventual success}\mid s\,], (3)

is the probability that a rollout of π\pi that passes through ss ends with a correct answer. An nn-gram connects the two views. We call the states in which the model emits gg the states marked by gg and write them sgs_{g}. The rollouts that contain gg are exactly those that pass through sgs_{g}, so the conditional accuracy of Section 3.2 estimates their average value, a⁡(g)≈Vπ​(sg)a(g)\approx V^{\pi}(s_{g}), and failure nn-grams mark low-value states. These states fall into two archetypes that share this value structure but differ in what is missing. In an unproductive behavior, the model reflects and then spirals rather than recovers: the pieces exist, but their composition fails. In a missing skill, the model stalls on an operation the subproblem requires, such as row reduction.

RL does little to repair such states. Under GRPO (Section 3.1), the policy learns how to continue from sgs_{g} only through the rollouts it samples there, and when Vπ​(sg)V^{\pi}(s_{g}) is low, few of them succeed. Section 4.4 bears this out: over RL, the rate at which rollouts enter the failure states stays flat, and the success rate from them rises only in step with overall accuracy (Figure 2), consistent with the small post-RL shifts reported by Wang et al. (2025b) and Zhao et al. (2025). Because on-policy sampling rarely produces the missing signal, we supply it before RL instead, by continued pretraining on text in which the failure nn-grams occur. This changes π0\pi_{0} itself, and with it both the policy that RL starts from and the reference of its KL penalty.

3.4 Repair: failure-nn-gram-guided continued pretraining

The repair has three steps. (i) Retrieve: each g∈𝒢g\in\mathcal{G} is an exact-match query to an infini-gram index (Liu et al., 2024) of the model’s pretraining and mid-training corpora. We extract a 2k-token window around every match, so that the text includes what surrounds the phrase, and sample documents with a per-query balanced budget of 3535M tokens in total unless stated otherwise. (ii) Continue pretraining: the base model is trained on the retrieved text with the next-token objective, either as released or, for OLMo2, after pretraining stage 1 and before mid-training (Section 4.1). (iii) Run RL: GRPO is re-run with all hyperparameters held fixed, so any difference is attributable to the CPT phase. The matched control runs the identical pipeline and budget with content-neutral queries (e.g., step 1), which separates the choice of text from the effect of continued pretraining itself.

4 Experiments

We now test the two claims of Section 3 empirically: that failure nn-grams localize where RL breaks, and that continued pretraining on text retrieved with them repairs it. The experiments span two model families, three RL settings of increasing breadth, and two insertion points, always against a matched control that receives the same pipeline and budget with content-neutral queries. Section 4.2 shows that RL failures concentrate in a small set of failure nn-grams; Section 4.3 shows that CPT guided by them raises the accuracy RL reaches over matched controls, most of all before mid-training; Section 4.4 shows that the deficit is conditional rather than a coverage gap; and Section 4.5 shows that 3535M tokens suffice.

4.1 Experimental setup

Models and tasks.

We study OLMo2 (Walsh et al., 2025) at 1B and 7B, as their pretraining and mid-training corpora are public, and Qwen3 (Yang et al., 2025) at 0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B, as they are among the best open-source small models. For OLMo2-1B we also use the public stage-1 checkpoint, taken before mid-training, which lets us insert the repair before mid-training. We always retrieve from the OLMo2 corpora, Olmo-mix and Dolmino-mix (Chen et al., 2026), for all models, including Qwen3, whose own corpus is not public; the Qwen3 runs therefore also test transfer across pretraining corpora. We consider three RL settings of increasing breadth: (i) GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021); (ii) a multi-task mixture of GSM8K, Social IQA (Sap et al., 2019), MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021), and TriviaQA (Joshi et al., 2017), mixed at a ratio of 8:2:1:18{:}2{:}1{:}1; and (iii) the General Reasoner setting (Ma et al., 2025), which trains on WebInstruct-verified prompts spanning math, science, and logic. All post-training uses GRPO, with G=5G=5 rollouts per prompt for (i) and (ii) (210 and 595 steps) and the General Reasoner recipe with G=8G=8 for (iii) (226 steps). Hyperparameters are held fixed between the runs with and without CPT.

Continued pretraining and controls.

For each setting we mine failure nn-grams from πRL\pi_{\mathrm{RL}} (Section 3.2), retrieve a corpus with a per-query balanced budget of 3535M tokens (larger budgets are studied in Section 4.5), and continue pretraining with the next-token objective before re-running RL. We study the effect of inserting CPT before and after OLMo2’s mid-training stage. Before mid-training: starting from the OLMo2-1B stage-1 checkpoint, CPT continues the stage-1 optimizer and schedule and is followed by a shortened stage-2 mid-training (0.84B tokens of the official Dolmino-mix, identical across conditions). After mid-training: CPT is run directly on the released base model with a fresh optimizer. The matched control runs the identical pipeline with the same budget but retrieves documents with content-neutral random queries.

Metrics.

We report greedy accuracy at the final RL step, without checkpoint selection. For GSM8K training we evaluate on the GSM8K test set; for the mixture we report the macro-average over the GSM8K test set, the MMLU validation set, TriviaQA, and the Social IQA test set; and for the General Reasoner setting we report the mean over GSM8K, MATH-500, Minerva, OlympiadBench, AMC, AIME 2024/25, and GPQA-Diamond, graded by normalized exact match with symbolic equivalence. For the marked states we measure, on the G=5G=5 training rollouts of a step (2560 rollouts), the conditional accuracy a⁡(g)a(g), the entry rate Pr⁡[Eg]\Pr[E_{g}], and the fraction of affected questions with a succeeding sibling rollout; we also report pass@kk up to k=32k=32. Numbers are single-seed unless marked; where we ran three RL seeds, the standard deviation across seeds is about one point.

4.2 Failure nn-grams localize RL failures

Across all models and settings, a small number of nn-grams predicts whether a rollout will fail. For OLMo2-1B on GSM8K, the failure five-grams of Table 1 appear in about 7%7\% of late-RL training rollouts, and those rollouts succeed 24%24\% of the time against 44%44\% for the rest (statistics are always measured on RL steps after the ones the nn-grams were mined from, to avoid selection bias). What the failure nn-grams contain shifts with model strength and task breadth (Table 1). For OLMo2-1B on GSM8K they are reflection and self-correction phrases (there’s a mistake, Let’s recheck); for Qwen3-4B on the mixture they are hedging phrases on the trivia questions (a more fitting answer, after careful consideration), with which the model talks itself out of an answer; and for the stronger Qwen3 models in the General Reasoner setting they are specific operations (convert the given matrix to [reduced row echelon form], use Coulomb’s [law]). The reflection phrases are not rare in pretraining data: each GSM8K retrieval query matches tens of thousands of Dolmino-mix documents (57,00057{,}000 at the median), whereas the highest-accuracy nn-grams of the same run (pizza is cut into) match about 950950. The model has seen let’s recheck many times; what it has not learned is what to do after saying it, so the behavioral deficit is unproductive use rather than absence. Table 1 also previews the repair: after CPT on text retrieved with these phrases, the model emits them more often and succeeds more often after them.

4.3 Targeted continued pretraining repairs RL

Table 2 reports the main result. With the RL recipe held fixed, inserting failure-nn-gram-guided CPT before RL gives the best final accuracy in every setting of the table, above both no CPT and the matched control. Over all GSM8K and multi-task settings we ran, it beats the control in 10 of 11 (9 with 35M tokens and 1 with 100M tokens; Table 5).33 3 The exceptions are in Table 8. The gain over the control is largest when the repair is inserted before mid-training: +2.0+2.0 on GSM8K over three RL seeds, where the control falls below no CPT. On released base models the gain is largest for the weakest model (+2.4+2.4 over the control for Qwen3-0.6B on GSM8K) and shrinks as the model gets stronger.

In the General Reasoner setting, where the failure nn-grams identify operations rather than behaviors, the corpus mined from Qwen3-4B and transferred to Qwen3-1.7B leads no CPT by +2.6+2.6, and continued pretraining alone, before any RL, raises Qwen3-4B’s eight-benchmark mean by 3.03.0 points while the same budget of random Olmo-mix text lowers it by 4.14.1.

4.4 The deficit is local, not a global coverage gap

Failing rollouts share questions with succeeding ones.

Late in RL (OLMo2-1B on GSM8K, steps 150–210), about 70 of the 512 prompts in each training batch have at least one rollout that enters a failure state, and for 46%46\% of these prompts another rollout of the same question reaches the correct answer. With only G=5G=5 samples per question this is a lower bound, so the correct answer is within the model’s reach for nearly half of the affected questions; what the model lacks is a way through the marked state, not the answer itself.

RL does not change how often the failure states are entered.

Figure 2 tracks the failure states over the course of RL. Training-rollout accuracy rises from 0.2%0.2\% to 47%47\% over 210 GRPO steps, but the fraction of rollouts that enter a failure state stays between 5%5\% and 7%7\% throughout (middle panel), and the success rate from those states rises at the same pace as overall accuracy (right panel). RL therefore improves the marked states only in proportion to everything else and does not single them out for repair (Wang et al., 2025b; Zhao et al., 2025).

RL does not expand coverage; CPT does, modestly.

Figure 3 plots pass@kk, the fraction of test questions solved by at least one of kk samples. Where the base model already produces the answer format (the middle and right panels), RL raises pass@1 by a large margin but pass@32 by only a few points, and on MATH-500 pass@32 after RL ends slightly below the base model’s (90.690.6 vs. 91.291.2), reproducing the finding of Yue et al. (2025) that RL makes the model sample its existing solutions more reliably rather than reach new ones. Continued pretraining before RL moves this ceiling, by a small amount. The repaired model has higher pass@kk than the matched control at every kk, and its pass@32 ends above the no-CPT run by 1.21.2 points on TriviaQA and 1.61.6 on MATH-500, where it is the only RL-trained model to finish above the base model (92.292.2). On TriviaQA its lead over the control grows with kk, from 1.61.6 points at k=1k{=}1 to 4.44.4 at k=32k{=}32, while its lead over no CPT stays near one point. In short, generic CPT shrinks the set of answers RL can reach, RL itself does not enlarge it, and targeted CPT enlarges it by one to two points at k=32k{=}32, at the edge of what 500 to 1000 test questions can resolve.

Targeted CPT makes the model enter the marked states more often and succeed from them more often.

Inserting our CPT after stage 1 and re-running the same RL recipe moves all three quantities of Table 3 in the intended direction. The entry rate into the failure states doubles, the success rate from them rises by about four points, and the share of affected questions with a correct sibling rollout rises from 46%46\% to 50%50\% (Figure 2, Table 3). The success rate rises in every other setting of Table 3 as well, most strongly for OLMo2-7B on the mixture. Two observations qualify this result: the matched control raises the success rate by a similar amount, though without raising the entry rate, and per phrase the reflection markers succeed 55–12%12\% of the time with or without the repair (Table 1; all 16 GSM8K queries in Table 15). What the repair changes most is therefore how often the model emits these phrases, so its accuracy gain cannot be attributed to the diagnosed states alone.

Missing skills are repaired more fully than unproductive behaviors.

The two archetypes of Section 3.3 respond differently to the same repair (Table 1). The operations that Qwen3-4B never completed correctly go from 0%0\% to 5050–62%62\% success after CPT, whereas the reflection phrases of OLMo2-1B move by only one or two points. A missing operation has a definite correct execution, which the retrieved text can supply directly, whereas a reflection phrase helps only if the model also knows what went wrong on the question at hand, which the retrieved recoveries do not teach. The repair therefore raises how often the model reflects far more than how often reflecting succeeds.

4.5 Analysis and ablations

Insert the repair before mid-training.

Table 4 compares the two insertion points at equal budget and with the identical pipeline. Inserted after stage 1, the targeted corpus is the best CPT data in both settings: on GSM8K it leads the matched control by +2.0+2.0 over three seeds, about two standard deviations, while generic text at the same budget falls below no CPT; on the mixture it leads no CPT by +2.6+2.6. Inserted into the released base model, the same corpus adds 1.31.3 points on GSM8K, but the matched control adds nearly as much, and on the mixture both CPT variants fall below no CPT. Two effects favor the earlier insertion: targeting only pays off before mid-training, and the mid-training that follows the repair absorbs the perturbation that CPT on a finished model leaves in place.

A small corpus is enough.

Table 5 varies the token budget. In every setting the gain appears at 3535–100100M tokens, and scaling the corpus to 11B leaves accuracy flat or lowers it. The cost of a large budget is sharpest before RL, where 11B tokens of retrieved text lowers Qwen3-4B’s eight-benchmark mean by 1919 points; mixing random documents into a large corpus does not recover the loss (Table 11).

The corpus transfers across model families.

The 3535M corpus mined from OLMo2-1B’s GSM8K failures improves Qwen3-0.6B on GSM8K by +2.4+2.4 over the control and Qwen3-4B on the mixture by +1.9+1.9 (Table 2), and in the other direction the corpus mined from Qwen3-4B’s General Reasoner failures lifts Qwen3-1.7B by +2.6+2.6 over no CPT (Table 2).

5 Conclusion

In this paper, we asked what specific capability a base model is missing when RL almost works, and whether it can be supplied before RL. Failure nn-grams read off the model’s own rollouts mark low-value states that on-policy, KL-anchored RL cannot self-repair. Using those nn-grams to retrieve and continue-pretrain on text that traverses the marked states improves downstream accuracy over matched controls when inserted before mid-training, and the corpus transfers across model families, all without labels or a teacher. A model’s own failures are an underused supervision signal: a cheap, label-free pointer to the pretraining data it needs most.

Appendix A Limitations

Several limitations scope our claims.

Effect sizes and evaluation.

Gains, while consistent in direction against no CPT across the GSM8K settings and most multi-task settings (and against the matched control in all but one), are modest in absolute terms (0.10.1–2.62.6 points); only the OLMo2-1B GSM8K conditions are averaged over three RL seeds, and some benchmarks (the small competition-math sets used in the General Reasoner setting) are high-variance. The seed standard deviation is about one point on GSM8K for a 1B model (Appendix D), so no single comparison exceeds two standard deviations, and the single-seed gains for the stronger Qwen3 models are not individually significant. In the General Reasoner setting, runs are compared at matched RL steps rather than at convergence. Stronger conclusions require more seeds and completed runs.

Dependence on open training corpora.

Our pipeline retrieves repair data from the base model’s own pretraining and mid-training corpora, which restricts it to model families that release this data (here, OLMo2). For Qwen3 we retrieve from Olmo’s corpora instead, which worked in our experiments but conflates corpus transfer with the repair itself. Applying the method to models with undisclosed corpora would in general require a substitute source of correct-traversal text—a public corpus indexed in place of the original, or synthetically generated traversals—which we do not study here.

Generic in-domain data is a strong baseline.

On an already mid-trained model, 3535M tokens of a curated math corpus (MegaMath-Web-Pro) matched our targeted corpus on GSM8K (Table 13). Targeting clearly beats matched generic data and is label-free, but when a high-quality in-domain corpus already exists, it is the cheaper option; our advantage is clearest before mid-training and for deficits with no obvious curated corpus (e.g., recovery from a self-identified error).

Simplicity of the retrieval signal.

We use exact-match nn-gram lookup via infini-gram, a deliberately lightweight instrument. It will miss relevant text that expresses the same marked state in different surface form (paraphrases, alternative notation, or different variable names), it can over-fragment a single long pattern into several near-duplicate nn-grams, and on task mixtures the lowest-accuracy nn-grams can be dominated by artifacts of individual sub-tasks (formatting fragments, rare tokens) rather than reasoning states, which we currently remove by hand. Retrieved spans also contain the trigger phrase more reliably than a completed recovery (Section 4.4). Denser or semantic retrieval seeded by the failure nn-grams, and filtering retrieved spans for the presence of a resolution, are natural extensions.

Associational, not causal, diagnosis.

The failure nn-grams mark low-value states rather than cause them: whether a rollout emits a given phrase is itself an outcome of the model’s state on that sample. We mitigate the most obvious confound by comparing rollouts of the same question with and without the nn-gram, but a fuller causal account—e.g., intervening to inject a marked phrase and measuring downstream success—remains open, and our claims should be read as identifying where failures concentrate rather than attributing causation to surface tokens.

Scope of the studied regime.

We focus on the regime where RL almost works—where the correct answer is often within the base model’s global support and the deficit is conditional recovery. Whether the same diagnose-and-repair recipe helps when the base model is far from competent (a genuine global coverage gap), how it composes over repeated diagnose–repair–RL cycles, and why large CPT budgets hurt when replay of the pretraining distribution does not repair them (Section 4.5), are questions we leave to future work.

Appendix B Hyperparameters

Mining and retrieval.

We mine nn-grams (n=3n=3–66) from the reasoning span of GRPO training rollouts at the final step (2560 rollouts per step, last 50 steps for the state-level statistics), keep those that occur at least 20 times and in at least 0.1%0.1\% of the rollouts, remove candidates dominated by digits or formatting, merge near-duplicates (Jaccard ≥0.9\geq 0.9) into their longest common span, and rank by accuracy. The lowest-accuracy 10–40 spans are used verbatim as exact-match queries to a local infini-gram index of Dolmino-mix and OLMoE-mix (DCLM and non-DCLM shards); each match is extracted with a 2000-token window, queries with fewer than 1000 matching documents are dropped, and documents are sampled with an equal per-query token budget (up-sampling a query’s pool at most once when it is exhausted).

Appendix C Retrieval queries behind every corpus

Table 7 lists, verbatim, the exact-match queries used to build each CPT corpus and control. Queries are the merged common spans of Section 3.2; truncated word pieces (e.g., stitute back) are kept as mined.

Appendix D Run-to-run variation

For OLMo2-1B on GSM8K we ran three RL seeds (different data order; vLLM sampling is not seeded) per condition with the CPT checkpoint fixed. Final-step accuracies are 36.2/38.2/37.936.2/38.2/37.9 (stage 1, no CPT), 35.6/35.8/37.135.6/35.8/37.1 (matched control), 39.2/38.9/36.539.2/38.9/36.5 (ours); 58.5/59.9/59.658.5/59.9/59.6 (released base, no CPT), 58.9/60.8/60.358.9/60.8/60.3 (random Olmo-mix), 58.1/60.1/60.058.1/60.1/60.0 (high-accuracy nn-grams), 60.7/59.6/61.560.7/59.6/61.5 (ours); and, over two seeds, 61.4/59.861.4/59.8 (trigger-only) and 59.9/60.359.9/60.3 (windows with a resolution). The standard deviation within a condition is 0.70.7–1.51.5 points, and the final-checkpoint accuracy of a single run fluctuates by 11–2.52.5 points between adjacent evaluation steps (e.g., 58.558.5 at step 210 vs. 61.061.0 at step 170). We therefore treat differences below about one point as null; the stage-1 gain over the matched control (+2.0+2.0) is about two standard deviations; the gain over no CPT (+0.8+0.8) is within noise. All other numbers in the paper are single-seed, except the OLMo2-1B multi-task no-CPT and ours entries (52.9/52.352.9/52.3 and 51.4/51.651.4/51.6 over two seeds; the mixture’s Social IQA component moves by three to five points between adjacent checkpoints, so single runs there carry about two points of noise).

Appendix E Additional results

Appendix F State-level effect of CPT across settings

Table 14 measures, for every base/CPT pair we trained, how often the RL policy enters the targeted failure states and how often it succeeds from them, before and after the repair. 𝒢\mathcal{G} is the set of retrieval queries used to build that pair’s CPT corpus (10–17 nn-grams), so the measurement asks exactly whether the states the corpus targeted became more recoverable. Both members of a pair are compared at the same RL step on the same prompts (the GG training rollouts of that step; for OLMo2-7B the validation generations). Accuracy is the sampled training-rollout accuracy at that step, not test accuracy.

Choice of RL steps.

The analysis sets of Table 1 and Figure 2 are mined in a window that starts after training-rollout accuracy has plateaued (OLMo2-1B on GSM8K: 33%33\% at step 100 vs. 36%36\% at 210; Qwen3-4B: 25%25\% at 120 vs. 26%26\% at 226) and ends before the scoring window, which is the last 60 steps shared by the compared runs: steps 120–140 and 150–210 (or 226) for the 210- and 226-step recipes, 480–520 and 535–595 for the 595-step multi-task recipe, and 50–60 and 80–104 for the Qwen3-1.7B runs, which stop at steps 103–105. The two windows are disjoint so that no nn-gram is scored on the rollouts that selected it (Section 4.4); they were fixed once per setting from the run length and not tuned. Rows that compare runs of different lengths (OLMo2-7B, 226 vs. 208 steps) use the last 27 steps of each run.

Across the three stage-1 RL seeds, the success rate from the failure states rises on every seed (+3.5+3.5, +5.5+5.5, +3.3+3.3) while the entry rate rises on seeds 1 and 2 and falls on seed 3, whose final test accuracy is also the one below no CPT (36.536.5 vs. 37.937.9).

Three patterns stand out. (i) Only the before-mid-training setting shows a rise in a⁡(𝒢)a(\mathcal{G}) together with an accuracy gain, and there the failure set is mined on steps 120–140 and evaluated on 150–210 to avoid the selection bias that a final-step comparison carries; the rise is modest (+6+6 points, control +2.5+2.5) and comes with a doubled entry rate. (ii) On released base models the targeted states are rare (≤2%\leq 2\% of rollouts) and the CPT corpus tends to make the model emit the trigger phrases more often (e.g., Qwen3-4B multi-task: still incorrect 0 →\to 162 occurrences at 36% accuracy), which raises the entry rate without raising the success rate. (iii) In the General Reasoner setting the self-mined operation nn-grams remain low-value after CPT, whereas the transferred corpus raises their value without changing accuracy, i.e., recoverability of a state and task accuracy can move independently.
